titre: The Ultimatum Game: From 26% to 58%, Depending on the People
accroche: In laboratories, the average offer hovers around 44%. In small-scale societies, it ranges from 26% to 58%.
contenu_vulgarise:
One player receives a sum equivalent to a day or two of local wages and offers a share to a second player. If the second player accepts, they split the sum as proposed. If the second player refuses, both walk away with nothing. According to the economic model of the selfish individual, the first player should offer the minimum and the second should accept any positive amount, since that beats zero.

This game, known as the ultimatum game, has been played hundreds of times by students, and the model fails: in industrialized societies, the average offer is close to 44%, the most common offer is 50%, and offers below 20% are rejected with a probability of 0.40 to 0.60. This uniformity left a question open: does it reflect universal behavior, or just the little cultural variation that students offer?

## Off Campus

In 2001, Joseph Henrich and a group of researchers played the same game in small-scale societies (fifteen, according to the title of their article), in the Amazon, Africa, Mongolia, and New Guinea. The selfish model fails everywhere, just as it does in the laboratory. But the gap between societies is much greater than the one seen between universities: average offers range from 26% among the Machiguenga of Peru to 58% among the people of Lamalera, Indonesia, a community of whale hunters. The Aché of Paraguay offer 51% on average.

Rejections vary too. The Machiguenga rejected only one offer, even though more than 75% of the offers were below 30%. The Hadza of Tanzania rejected 24% of all offers, and 43% of those of 20% or less. Among the Au and the Gnau of Papua New Guinea, offers that are too low and offers that are too generous, above 50%, are refused almost equally often.

## What Explains the Gap

In the full 2005 version, published in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, the authors analyze the gap. Individual economic and demographic variables do not explain behavior consistently, either within groups or between them. What matters is collective life: the more a society is integrated into the market, and the more cooperation pays off in daily life, the higher the offers climb. Behavior in the game often reflects everyday habits.

## An Unusual Sample

In 2010, Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan took up the finding on a large scale in Behavioral and Brain Sciences. The behavioral sciences publish general claims based on samples drawn almost entirely from Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, hence the acronym WEIRD (which also means “strange”). Their review shows that these subjects are often outliers compared with the rest of the species. Nine domains are reviewed, from visual perception to the heritability of IQ, by way of fairness and cooperation.

repere.texte: In the ultimatum game, the average offer is close to 44% in industrialized societies, and ranges from 26% (Machiguenga, Peru) to 58% (Lamalera, Indonesia) in the sample of small-scale societies.
repere.source: Henrich et al., “In Search of Homo Economicus: Behavioral Experiments in 15 Small-Scale Societies,” American Economic Review, 91 (2), 2001, pp. 73–78

carte.punch: Same game, same rules: the average offer ranges from 26% to 58% depending on the people.
carte.idee: The ultimatum game yields an average offer of nearly 44% among students. Henrich et al. (2001) played it in small-scale societies: from 26% among the Machiguenga to 58% in Lamalera. Subjects from Western, rich, industrialized countries are often outliers.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Henrich et al., “In Search of Homo Economicus,” open-access text (University of Munich)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Text of the 2001 article, with Table 1 of average offers and rejection rates by society.

quiz.question: What does the ultimatum game played in small-scale societies reveal, compared with the version played by students?
choix: That players everywhere offer the lowest possible amount, as the economic model predicts
That all peoples offer half, which would prove a universal fairness
That average offers vary far more from one society to another than students alone had shown
That generous offers are always accepted, since they pay the second player more
quiz.explication: The selfish model fails everywhere, but averages range from 26% to 58% depending on the society, a far wider gap than among students. Nobody offers the minimum on average, not all societies offer 50%, and among the Au and the Gnau offers above 50% are often refused.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do the Machiguenga of Peru react to low offers in the 2001 study?
choix: They reject nearly all offers below 30%
They rejected only a single offer, even though more than 75% of the offers received were below 30%
They systematically reject offers above 50%, judged too generous
They refuse to play when the offer is less than half
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that the Machiguenga rejected only a single offer, even though more than 75% of the offers they received were below 30%: a very low rejection rate despite low offers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Among the Au and the Gnau of Papua New Guinea, what peculiarity is observed in rejections?
choix: They never refuse any offer, whatever the amount
They refuse only offers below 10%
They refuse offers that are too generous almost as often as those that are too low
They refuse all offers equal to 50%, judged arbitrary
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry specifies that among the Au and the Gnau, offers that are too generous, above 50%, are refused almost as often as offers that are too low, the opposite of what a model based on individual self-interest predicts.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to the 2005 analysis published in Behavioral and Brain Sciences, what best explains the gap in average offers between societies?
choix: The individual education level of each participant in the experiment
The size of the total sum offered at the start of each round of the game
The average age of the participants recruited in each society studied
The society's integration into the market and the everyday payoffs of cooperation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry states that individual economic and demographic variables do not explain behavior consistently, whereas integration into the market and the everyday payoffs of cooperation push offers higher.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the acronym WEIRD, used by Henrich, Heine, and Norenzayan in 2010, stand for?
choix: Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies
Poor, rural, isolated societies without markets
Societies drawn exclusively from Africa and Asia
The fifteen small-scale societies studied in 2001
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The entry explains that WEIRD refers to Western, educated, industrialized, rich, and democratic societies, from which most behavioral-science samples are drawn, and that these subjects are often outliers.
